text: The last piece of the capstone's spec is the one that's easy to skip but arguably the most important: a written, gate-by-gate explanation of how the state evolved. This lesson writes that explanation for the GHZ circuit, then closes out the course by connecting every chapter back to this one small project.

Before any gate, all three qubits start in |0>, entirely amplitude 1.0 on label 000. After h(0), the Hadamard puts qubit 0 into equal superposition while qubits 1 and 2 stay untouched: 0.7071068 on 000 and on 001. There's no entanglement yet — just one qubit in superposition. After cx(0,1), the 001 branch, where qubit 0 is 1, flips qubit 1, turning it into 011 — entanglement is created, qubits 0 and 1 now agree with each other in every branch. After cx(1,2), the 011 branch, where qubit 1 is 1, flips qubit 2, completing the GHZ state at 000 and 111.

Step back from the individual numbers. The single Hadamard created the only superposition in the whole circuit. Every CX gate after that did one specific job: extending the existing split to one more qubit, so that qubit becomes perfectly correlated with the branch it's propagating from. No new superposition was ever created — the two amplitudes stayed at 0.7071068 throughout. That's the general recipe for an n-qubit GHZ state at any size: one Hadamard, then a chain of CX gates, each one's control equal to the previous qubit in the chain.

Look back at what this one small project actually required. Building the circuit from a plain-Python spec is Chapter 2's territory. Running it two ways is Chapter 3's Aer simulator and statevector-versus-shots distinction. The histograms and state visualizations you'd use to eyeball these results are Chapter 4's tools. The reason a real device wouldn't give you a clean split traces back to Chapter 5's hardware realities and Chapter 7's noise and mitigation techniques. And the gate-by-gate bookkeeping you just walked through is the same bookkeeping, repeated far more times with far more structure, that makes an algorithm like Grover's from Chapter 6 work.

That's the real takeaway to leave this course with. A quantum circuit, no matter how sophisticated the algorithm built from it, is still just a sequence of gates moving amplitudes around a statevector, one step at a time — traceable by hand for small cases, and trusted to Qiskit's engine at scale. You've now built, and validated, a small tool that does exactly that tracing and trusting for you.
That closes out Quantum Programming with Qiskit — from your very first one-line circuit in Lesson 1 to a validated capstone tool built on every chapter in between.
